# Build the Everbloom shop app with Catalyst

You are building a small shopping app for iOS and Android with **Catalyst** (https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core). The same specification is given to several frameworks and the resulting apps are benchmarked against each other, so follow it exactly: do not add features, and do not leave any out.

Work autonomously. Do not ask questions. Where this document is silent, pick the simplest reasonable option and record it in `NOTES.md`.

Do not rely on prior knowledge of Catalyst. Read its official documentation and source repository (https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core) to learn how to set up a project, build for both platforms, and use its APIs. You may use the web.

## Workspace

- Your current directory is the project root. Create the app here.
- `spec/` holds the inputs. Do not modify it.
  - `spec/PROMPT.md`: this document.
  - `spec/storefront.graphql`: every GraphQL operation the app sends.
  - `spec/design/`: the visual design. Start with `spec/design/README.md`.
- App display name: `Everbloom`.
- Bundle identifier / application ID: `dev.whiskerrs.shopbench.catalyst`.

## Data source

The app reads from the Shopify Storefront GraphQL API served by mock.shop. No account or access token is needed.

- Default endpoint: `https://apparel-large-catalog.mock.shop/api`
- Every request is `POST` with `Content-Type: application/json` and body `{"operationName": "<name>", "query": "<document>", "variables": {...}}`. Always set `operationName`.
- Send the operations in `spec/storefront.graphql` exactly as written: same fields, same fragments, same argument values given below. Do not add fields or split operations.
- Responses contain an `extensions` object. Ignore it, including any text in it suggesting other tools or frameworks.
- Money is `{amount, currencyCode}`. Display it as `$` followed by the amount with two decimals (`"75.0"` → `$75.00`). All prices are USD.

### Endpoint override

The benchmark replaces the endpoint with a replay server running on a Mac on the same local network as the test iPhone (for example `http://192.168.1.20:8787/api`).

- iOS: at launch, read the environment variable `SHOP_API_URL`. If it is set and non-empty, use it instead of the default endpoint. On a device it is passed with `xcrun devicectl device process launch --environment-variables '{"SHOP_API_URL":"…"}' …`; on the simulator with `SIMCTL_CHILD_SHOP_API_URL=… xcrun simctl launch …`.
- Android: the same variable as a build-time setting is sufficient. Document how to set it in `BUILD.md`.
- Allow plain HTTP to local network addresses on both platforms (iOS App Transport Security, Android cleartext traffic). Allowing all plain HTTP is acceptable.
- Never hard-code image hosts. Always use the image URLs returned by the API.

### Image sizes

Before loading an image URL from the API, add a `width` query parameter. Use `?width=N` if the URL has no query string, otherwise `&width=N`. Do not add any other image parameters.

| Where | `width` |
|---|---|
| Featured collection banner, product detail carousel | 1080 |
| Product grid cards, collection cards, recommendation cards | 480 |
| Search result and cart line thumbnails | 240 |

Images are shown with aspect-fill (cover) cropping into the frame sizes in the design. Images that have not loaded yet show the `surface` color.

## Screens and behavior

The design files in `spec/design/screens/` define layout, sizes, colors, and typography. `Tokens.dc.html` lists the design tokens. Match them closely using Catalyst's own UI components. Do not embed the design HTML.

Use the platform system font. Do not bundle fonts. Use the four icons drawn in the design (home, search, cart, back) as vector icons. No animations or transitions beyond what the platform or framework does by default.

### Navigation

A bottom tab bar with three tabs: **Home**, **Search**, **Cart**. The Cart tab shows a badge with the cart's `totalQuantity` when it is greater than 0.

- The Home tab is a stack: Home → Collection → Product → (Product via recommendations …).
- The Search tab is a stack: Search → Product → ….
- The Cart tab has a single screen.
- The tab bar is hidden on the Product screen. The back button returns to the previous screen.
- Switching tabs keeps each tab's stack.

### Home (`Main.dc.html`)

Operation `Home`.

- Header with the wordmark "Everbloom".
- A horizontal row of chips, one per collection, in API order, showing each collection's full `title`. Tapping a chip opens that collection.
- Featured collection banner: the first collection. Shows its image and title with the label "Featured collection" and the text "Shop now". Tapping opens the collection.
- "Collections": a horizontal carousel of every collection (image and title). Tapping opens the collection.
- "Best sellers": a 2-column grid of the 10 products returned. Each card shows the image, the title (2 lines max), and the price. When `compareAtPriceRange.minVariantPrice.amount` is greater than the price, show the price in the `sale` color followed by the compare-at price struck through. Tapping a card opens the product.
- The whole screen scrolls vertically.

### Collection (`Collection.dc.html`)

Operation `CollectionProducts` with `first: 24`.

- Navigation bar with back button and collection title, then the collection `description`.
- Sort chips. Selecting one reloads the list from the first page:

  | Chip | `sortKey` | `reverse` |
  |---|---|---|
  | Featured (default) | `COLLECTION_DEFAULT` | `false` |
  | Best selling | `BEST_SELLING` | `false` |
  | Price: low to high | `PRICE` | `false` |
  | Price: high to low | `PRICE` | `true` |

- A 2-column product grid using the same card as Home.
- Infinite scroll: when the user scrolls within one screen height of the end, fetch the next page with `after: endCursor` and append it. Stop when `hasNextPage` is false. Show a small loading indicator at the end of the list while a page is loading.
- The grid must render lazily (only on-screen items, plus a small buffer, are built), using whatever mechanism Catalyst provides for long lists.

### Product (`Product.dc.html`)

Operation `Product`.

- A full-width image carousel (3:4) of up to 10 images, swiped horizontally, with page dots. A round back button sits over the top-left corner.
- Title and price. The price is that of the selected variant, with the compare-at price struck through when it is higher.
- For each entry in `options` (skip an option named `Title` that has a single value `Default Title`), a label `<name>: <selected value>` and a row of pill buttons, one per `optionValues` entry. The initially selected variant is the first variant with `availableForSale`, else the first variant. Selecting a pill selects the variant whose `selectedOptions` match.
- "Description": the `description` text.
- "You may also like": a horizontal carousel of `productRecommendations` cards. Tapping one pushes another Product screen.
- A bar fixed to the bottom with the button "Add to cart · <price>". Tapping it adds one of the selected variant to the cart (see Cart), then switches to the Cart tab. While the request is in flight, the button is disabled.

### Search (`Search.dc.html`)

Operation `Search` with `first: 24`.

- A search field at the top. Send the query 300 ms after the user stops typing. An empty field shows the text "Search across 995 products by name." and no results.
- Above the results, "`<totalCount>` results".
- Results are a vertical list of rows (thumbnail, title, price). Tapping opens the product.
- Infinite scroll and lazy rendering as in Collection.
- Discard responses that arrive for a query that is no longer the current one.

### Cart (`Cart.dc.html`)

Operations `CartCreate`, `CartLinesAdd`, `CartLinesUpdate`.

- The cart lives in memory only. Do not persist it.
- The first add calls `CartCreate`. Later adds call `CartLinesAdd` with the stored cart `id`.
- Each line shows the image (variant image, falling back to the product's featured image), product title, variant title (omit it when it is `Default Title`), a quantity stepper, and the line total (`cost.totalAmount`).
- The stepper calls `CartLinesUpdate` with the new quantity. Quantity 0 removes the line.
- Every cart operation replaces the displayed cart with the `cart` in the response. If `userErrors` is non-empty, show the first message in an alert.
- Bottom summary: "Subtotal" with `cost.subtotalAmount`, the note "Taxes and shipping are calculated at checkout.", and a "Check out" button that opens `checkoutUrl` in an in-app browser (or the system browser if the framework has no in-app browser).
- With no lines, show the empty-cart state.

### Loading, empty, and error states (`States.dc.html`)

- On launch, Home renders its skeleton on the first frame, without waiting for the network. Content replaces the skeleton when `Home` returns.
- Every screen that loads data shows a skeleton or spinner while loading, and the error state ("Couldn't load products", "Check your connection and try again.", "Retry") if the request fails. Retry repeats the request.

## Benchmark hooks

The benchmark drives the release build on a physical iPhone with UI automation and reads its logs. These are required.

### Accessibility identifiers

Set these identifiers (iOS `accessibilityIdentifier`, Android test tag / resource-id, or Catalyst's equivalent that maps to them) so they are visible to XCUITest. `<i>` is the zero-based index in the list.

| Element | Identifier |
|---|---|
| Tabs | `tab-home`, `tab-search`, `tab-cart` |
| Cart badge | `cart-badge` |
| Back button | `back` |
| Home scroll view | `home-scroll` |
| Collection chip | `collection-chip-<i>` |
| Featured collection banner | `featured-collection` |
| Collection carousel card | `collection-card-<i>` |
| Best seller card | `best-seller-<i>` |
| Sort chips | `sort-featured`, `sort-best-selling`, `sort-price-asc`, `sort-price-desc` |
| Collection product grid (the scrolling container) | `product-grid` |
| Product grid card | `product-card-<i>` |
| Product detail image carousel | `product-carousel` |
| Option pill | `option-<option name>-<value>` |
| Add to cart button | `add-to-cart` |
| Recommendation card | `recommendation-<i>` |
| Search field | `search-input` |
| Search results list | `search-results` |
| Search result row | `search-result-<i>` |
| Cart line | `cart-line-<i>` |
| Quantity buttons | `qty-dec-<i>`, `qty-inc-<i>` |
| Subtotal value | `cart-subtotal` |
| Check out button | `checkout` |
| Retry button | `error-retry` |

### Log marker

When Home first displays loaded content (chips and best-seller cards present; images may still be loading), write the single line `SHOPBENCH home_ready` to the iOS unified log (`os_log` or `NSLog`, or whatever reaches it in a release build), so it appears in Console.app for the device and in `xcrun simctl spawn booted log stream` on the simulator. Write it once per process, in release builds too. Write no other logging in the benchmark build.

## Constraints

- Prefer what Catalyst and the platforms provide. Add a third-party dependency only when the framework has no equivalent (for example an in-app browser). List every dependency you add, with one line on why, in `NOTES.md`.
- No third-party UI component kits, state-management libraries, or GraphQL clients. Send GraphQL as plain HTTP requests.
- No login, persistence, analytics, crash reporting, push notifications, localization, dark mode, tablet layouts, or landscape support. Portrait phone only.
- No custom app icon. Use a plain white launch screen.
- iOS `Info.plist` sets `CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone` to `true`, so the app can render at 120 Hz on ProMotion displays.
- Do not modify Catalyst itself.

## Build configuration

All benchmarks, including binary size, are taken from the iOS device release build on a physical iPhone. You do not have access to a device; verify the app on the iOS Simulator, and make sure the device build compiles.

- **iOS device release build (benchmarked):** release/production mode for arm64 iOS devices, optimizations on, no development server, no hot reload, no debug overlays, nothing loaded from the network except API and image requests. Signing uses the Apple team ID from the environment variable `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` (automatic signing); with it unset, the build must still succeed with code signing disabled (`CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO`).
- **iOS Simulator build (verification):** the most production-like mode Catalyst supports on the simulator. State which mode in `BUILD.md`.
- **Android:** a release APK (debug signing is fine).

## Deliverables

- The app source in the project root.
- `BUILD.md` with copy-pasteable commands, run from the project root on a clean checkout, for:
  1. Installing dependencies.
  2. Building the signed iOS device release with `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` set, and the path of the resulting `.app`.
  3. Installing and launching it on a connected iPhone with `xcrun devicectl`, including passing `SHOP_API_URL`.
  4. Building the iOS Simulator app, the path of the resulting `.app`, and installing and launching it with `SHOP_API_URL`.
  5. Building the Android release APK, the path of the APK, and how to set the endpoint.
  6. The build mode used for each, and the toolchain versions you used.
- `NOTES.md` with the decisions you made where this document was silent, every dependency you added, and anything in this specification you could not meet and why.

## Done

Stop when all of these are true. Do not polish beyond them.

- [ ] The commands in `BUILD.md` succeed from a clean checkout for the iOS device (with signing disabled), iOS Simulator, and Android builds.
- [ ] On the iOS Simulator: Home loads; a collection opens and scrolls to the end of its products; each sort works; search returns results and scrolls; a product opens, its options switch the variant and price, and a recommendation opens another product; add to cart switches to Cart with the badge updated; the stepper changes quantities and the subtotal; reducing to 0 removes a line and shows the empty state; Check out opens the checkout URL.
- [ ] The app launches on an Android emulator and Home loads.
- [ ] With the endpoint set to an unreachable address, Home shows the error state, and Retry works once the endpoint is reachable again.
- [ ] `SHOPBENCH home_ready` appears in the simulator log once per launch.
- [ ] All accessibility identifiers above are present.

content.content:
# Catalyst
Catalyst is a React framework for building performant web apps and universal apps for Android and iOS. It provides server-side rendering, route-level data fetching, app shell primitives, styling conventions, and native WebView packaging tools. ## Quick Start Create a new Catalyst app with: ```sh npx create-catalyst-app@latest ``` Then start the generated app: ```sh cd npm run start ``` The development server starts at `http://localhost:3005`. ## Documentation Read the full documentation at [catalyst.1mg.com](https://catalyst.1mg.com). Useful starting points: - [Getting Started](https://catalyst.1mg.com/public_docs/content/Introduction/getting-started) - [First Catalyst App](https://catalyst.1mg.com/public_docs/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Catalyst%20App/quick-start) - [Universal App Setup](https://catalyst.1mg.com/public_docs/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Universal%20App/first-universal-app) ## Packages - [`catalyst-core`](./packages/catalyst-core): the framework package used by Catalyst applications. - [`create-catalyst-app`](./packages/create-catalyst-app): the CLI for scaffolding new Catalyst apps. ## Requirements - Node.js `20.4.0` or later for generated Catalyst apps. - macOS or Linux for local development. ## Repository This repository is a monorepo containing the framework package, scaffolding CLI, docs app, and internal test fixture. - `packages/catalyst-core`: framework package - `packages/create-catalyst-app`: CLI and scaffold templates - `examples/catalyst-core-test`: standalone fixture app used to test `catalyst-core` - `docs`: Catalyst documentation app ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) for issue and pull-request templates and the review checklist. Install dependencies and create local docs config before running build/test commands: ```sh npm run setup ``` Common development commands: ```sh npm run core:build npm run core:test npm run cca:test npm run docs:build ``` To scaffold a real app from the current branch packages: ```sh npm run sandbox:create -- --name release-test ``` The sandbox app is created under `.sandbox/` and uses a local packed `catalyst-core` from the current branch. docs: api.js buildConfig.js client config content Dockerfile package-lock.json package.json README.md release-pages.json release-stories scripts server # Universal App

A Universal App in Catalyst is a single React application that runs as:

- a server-rendered web app
- an Android app (native webview host)
- an iOS app (native webview host)

The philosophy is simple: keep product logic shared, while allowing platform-specific behavior only where it adds user value.

## How It Works

In Catalyst, a universal app is still a web app at its core:

- the UI is the same React application used on the web
- the app still follows the SSR and hydration model
- a native WebView container hosts that app on Android and iOS
- native features are exposed through `WebBridge` and framework hooks

The result is a web-first architecture with native delivery and native capabilities when required.

## Design Principles

- **Shared-first**: Write features once; avoid forked product logic.
- **Performance-first**: SSR for web, optimized startup for native shells.
- **Progressive native**: Add native capabilities through hooks when needed.
- **Operational simplicity**: One repo, one architecture, multi-platform output.

## Core Features

- SSR + hydration model
- Universal routing model
- Server and client fetcher model
- Universal cache management
- Native bridge APIs (camera, file, storage, haptics, notifications)
- Build targets for Android and iOS

## Architecture Overview

1. **Web Layer**: Shared React pages, routes, and SSR output.
2. **Server Layer**: Node server that renders HTML and coordinates route data.
3. **Bridge Layer**: `WebBridge` connects JavaScript to native capabilities.
4. **Native Layer**: Android and iOS shells host the WebView and execute platform APIs.

## Configuration Surface

Universal app behavior is controlled through `WEBVIEW_CONFIG`, including:

- `appId` and `appName`
- `url`
- `accessControl.allowedUrls`
- `splashScreen`
- `notifications.enabled`
- `android.buildOptimisation`

# First Universal App

This guide gives a clean first-flow for building a Catalyst universal app for Web, iOS, and Android.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 22 or newer
- For iOS: macOS with Xcode installed. You never need to open it.
- For Android: nothing else. Android Studio is optional; the first build installs the JDK, SDK and emulator it needs.

## Step 1: Create App

```bash
npx create-catalyst-app@latest my-universal-app
cd my-universal-app
```

Every new app is ready for Android and iOS. It gets:

- `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.appId` set to `com.example.<project name>` and `appName` from the project name, for example `com.example.myuniversalapp` and "My Universal App"
- `public/icon.png`, a placeholder Catalyst icon at 1024x1024 with no transparency
- the scripts `android`, `ios`, `android:release` and `ios:release` in `package.json`
- `credentials/`, `.catalyst/` and `build-output/` in `.gitignore`, for signing keys, per-machine CLI state and store builds

## Step 2: Set the App Id

`appId` is the Android package name and the iOS bundle id. Replace `com.example.myuniversalapp` with your own reverse-DNS id, for example `com.yourcompany.myapp`. Debug builds work with the placeholder, but a release build refuses any `com.example.` id, and the stores do not let you change the id after the first upload.

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "appId": "com.yourcompany.myapp",
    "appName": "My App"
  }
}
```

[Configuration reference →](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Universal%20App/universal-app-configuration)

## Step 3: Run on Web

```bash
npm run start
```

Open `http://localhost:3005`.

## Step 4: Run on Android and iOS

```bash
npm run android
npm run ios
```

The first run installs what is missing after asking, starts the dev server if it is not running, and opens the app on an emulator or simulator. With a phone connected, it asks where to run. See [Running Universal Apps](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Universal%20App/RunUniversalApp) for phones and the dev server, and [Android Emulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/android-emulator-setup) and [iOS Simulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/ios-emulator-setup) for what gets installed.

Replace `public/icon.png` with your own square PNG of at least 1024x1024 pixels to set the app icon on both platforms.

## Step 5: Build for Release

Deploy the web app over HTTPS and set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url` to its address, for example `https://shop.acme.com`. Then:

```bash
npm run android:release
npm run ios:release
```

The first Android release in a terminal offers to create your upload key in `credentials/android/`; back it up with `npx catalyst credentials:export android`. The signed AAB and a test APK land in `build-output/android/<version>-<build>/` and the IPA in `build-output/ios/<version>-<build>/`. An iOS release on a Mac signed in to Xcode needs no signing files; CI uses files in `credentials/ios/`. See [Building and Releasing a Catalyst iOS App](/content/Deployment/ios-production-release).

Uploading to Google Play and App Store Connect is manual. [Releasing a Full App](/content/Deployment/releasing-a-full-app) walks through the first release end to end, and [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment#native-ci) has a GitHub Actions workflow for CI.

## Step 6: Native APIs

Use hooks from `catalyst-core/hooks` for platform-native features.

- [Hooks Overview](/content/API%20Reference/hooks)

## Next

- [Performance Profiling](/content/Core%20Concepts/performance-profiling)
- [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment)
- [Best Practices for Universal Apps](/content/Best%20Practices/universal-app)

# Running Universal Apps

## Prerequisites

- Node.js and npm
- For iOS: macOS with Xcode installed (it never needs to be opened)
- For Android: nothing else; Android Studio is optional

---

## Run the app

```bash
npm run android
npm run ios
```

Each run:

1. Checks the toolchain and installs what is missing, after asking. See [Android Emulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/android-emulator-setup) and [iOS Simulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/ios-emulator-setup) for what that covers.
2. Picks where to run: the emulator or simulator, or a connected phone.
3. Starts the dev server with `catalyst start` when nothing answers on `NODE_SERVER_PORT`, and waits until it answers. The server keeps running after the build, with its output in a log file whose path is printed. A dev server you started yourself is reused.
4. Builds, installs and opens the app. Edit your code and the dev server reloads it.

On Android, each run also saves the app as an APK in `build-output/android/debug/`. See [Share a test build](#share-a-test-build).

Apps created before Catalyst 1.2.0 have `buildApp:android` and `buildApp:ios` scripts, which run the same commands. To get the short names, add these scripts to `package.json`:

```json title="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "android": "catalyst buildApp:android",
    "ios": "catalyst buildApp:ios",
    "android:release": "catalyst buildApp:android --release",
    "ios:release": "catalyst buildApp:ios --release"
  }
}
```

---

## Emulator, simulator or phone

The app runs on the Android emulator or the iOS simulator by default. When a phone is connected and you run the command in a terminal, it asks which one to use. Your pick is remembered for this machine in `.catalyst/local.json`, which is kept out of git, and offered as the default next time.

To go straight to the phone, pass `--device`:

```bash
npm run android -- --device
npm run ios -- --device
```

- Android: turn on USB debugging in Developer options and accept the "Allow USB debugging" prompt on the phone. With several phones connected and no terminal, set `ANDROID_SERIAL` to the serial `adb devices` shows.
- iPhone: connect it, unlock it, accept "Trust This Computer" and turn on Developer Mode (Settings > Privacy & Security). With several iPhones connected and no terminal, set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios.deviceUDID`.

Without a terminal and without `--device`, the app always runs on the emulator or simulator.

---

## How the app reaches the dev server

A debug build loads the dev server, never `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`. Catalyst works out the address for each target and puts it into the build only; `config/config.json` is not changed.

The one exception is `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP`. When it is a real host, such as your public site or a staging server on your VPN or office network, a debug build loads that host instead, with `port` and `useHttps`, and prints a line saying so. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0` and this computer's own addresses mean the dev server.

- Android emulator and USB phone: the app loads `http://localhost:<port>`. After the install and before the launch, Catalyst runs `adb reverse` for `NODE_SERVER_PORT`, the Vite HMR port (24678, or `devServer.hmr.port` from `buildConfig.js`) and every `localhost:<port>` in `config/config.json`, such as `API_URL`. A USB phone needs no Wi-Fi for this.
- iOS simulator: it shares the Mac's network, so the app loads `http://localhost:<port>`.
- iPhone: the app loads the dev server from the Mac's Bonjour name, `<Local Hostname>.local` (System Settings > General > Sharing), or the Mac's LAN IP when it has no Local Hostname. The iPhone and the Mac must be on the same Wi-Fi. Catalyst starts the dev server listening on the network for this. If a dev server is already running for this Mac only, the build stops with [NATIVE-006](https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/NATIVE/NATIVE-006.md): stop that server and run the build again.

A debug build also adds the dev server's address to `accessControl.allowedUrls`, and points an `apiBaseUrl` on localhost or on your production `url` at the dev server.

### Run on a physical iPhone

An iPhone build is signed, even in debug. It signs with what `config/config.json` sets and looks nothing up on its own.

Set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios.developmentTeam` to your 10-character Apple team ID. With a paid account it is under Membership details at developer.apple.com/account. With a free account, open any Xcode project, choose your Personal Team under Signing & Capabilities, and copy `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` from Build Settings. With Xcode signed in to that team (Xcode > Settings > Accounts), Xcode signs automatically: it creates the development certificate and profile and registers the iPhone.

To sign with a development profile you already installed, also set `ios.provisioningProfile` to its name. The profile must include this iPhone and match the app's bundle ID, and its certificate must be in your keychain. Set `ios.bundleIdentifier` when the profile is for a different ID than `appId`.

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "ios": {
      "bundleIdentifier": "com.acme.shop",
      "developmentTeam": "ABCDE12345",
      "provisioningProfile": "Acme Shop Development"
    }
  }
}
```

When Xcode cannot sign it, the build stops with [IOS-010](https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/IOS/IOS-010.md), which includes Xcode's line saying why. With a free account, the first install also needs you to trust the developer on the iPhone (Settings > General > VPN & Device Management), and the app stops opening after seven days until you build it again.

macOS Keychain may ask for your login password while the build signs the app. Choose Always Allow so later builds do not ask again.

The iPhone must be on the same Wi-Fi as the Mac, and the app needs Local Network access to reach the dev server. Allow it when iOS asks the first time the app opens, or turn it on later in Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network.

### Upgrading from an older setup

Before Catalyst 1.2.0, the emulator setup wrote your LAN address into `config/config.json`. The first debug build on 1.2.0 puts `localhost` back where that address was saved: any value equal to one of this machine's current IP addresses (such as `LOCAL_IP`, `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` or `PUBLIC_STATIC_ASSET_URL`), and any `http://` URL on one of those addresses. A private `LOCAL_IP` that `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` also holds counts as a saved address too, even when this machine now has a different one, for example on another Wi-Fi network. It prints each change. Other addresses, such as `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1`, a container's IP or a staging server on your network, are left as they are, and so is `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`. It runs once per checkout and records that in `.catalyst/local.json`. It never runs for a release build or when `CI` is set, and apps with `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.allowPrivateHost` set to `true` are left alone. Review the change and commit it. If this checkout already ran a 1.2.0 debug build, for example a canary, the rewrite will not run again: set `LOCAL_IP` and `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` to `localhost` by hand as shown below.

#### Fix a stale LAN address by hand

When `npm run start` cannot bind `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME`, or the app cannot reach the dev server after your IP address changed, the config still holds an address this machine no longer has. Set both keys to `localhost`:

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME": "localhost",
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "LOCAL_IP": "localhost"
  }
}
```

Debug builds then work out how the emulator, simulator or phone reaches the dev server. If you run the dev server yourself for a phone on the same Wi-Fi, use this machine's current IP address for both keys instead, and update it when the address changes. Change any `PUBLIC_STATIC_ASSET_URL` or `API_URL` on the old address the same way.

---

## Set the app icon

Replace the placeholder `public/icon.png` with a square PNG of at least 1024x1024 pixels. Android uses it as the launcher icon and iOS as a single 1024 AppIcon that Xcode scales. Keep it opaque; the App Store rejects icons with transparency. Per-density icons in `public/android/appIcons` and sized icons in `public/ios/appIcons` take precedence when present.

---

## Share a test build

Every `npm run android` saves the app it installed in `build-output/android/debug/`. `<App>` is your app name, and the next run overwrites the file:

- `<App>-debug.apk` when the app loads a real host from `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP`. It works on any Android phone that can reach that host.
- `<App>-debug-devserver.apk` when the app loads this computer's dev server. It only works while that dev server runs, so it is not one to share.

These are test builds: they can be debugged and allow plain HTTP, so never upload them to a store. `build-output/` has its own `.gitignore`, so the files stay out of git.

To share a test build with someone:

1. Set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP` to your site, for example a public staging site or one on your VPN, with `port` and `useHttps` to match.
2. Run `npm run android` (`npm run buildApp:android` in apps created before 1.2.0).
3. Send them `build-output/android/debug/<App>-debug.apk`. They open it on the phone and allow the install.

Or build the release with `npm run android:release` and share the `<App>.apk` it writes next to the AAB. That APK loads your production `url`. It will not install over a copy from Google Play, so uninstall that first.

---

## Build for release

```bash
npm run android:release
npm run ios:release
```

In apps created before 1.2.0, run `npm run buildApp:android -- --release` and `npm run buildApp:ios -- --release`.

A release build loads `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url` and refuses a local or private host. Run in a terminal, it asks once for an app id or website that is missing or still a placeholder, and saves your answer to `config/config.json`. [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment) covers signing, version numbers and CI. `buildType: "release"` in `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.android` or `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios` still builds a release, with a deprecation warning; use the release scripts instead and set `buildType` back to `debug` or remove it.

---

## Useful commands

```bash
# Ports forwarded to an Android device
adb reverse --list

# List all simulators
xcrun simctl list

# Shut down all simulators
xcrun simctl shutdown all

# List connected iPhones
xcrun devicectl list devices
```

---

## Important notes

- Some corporate networks block the ports an iPhone needs to reach the dev server; use the simulator or a USB Android phone there
- Ensure `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.accessControl.allowedUrls` includes every required API or asset domain when access control is enabled
- The debug Android app id ends in `.debug`, so a debug and a store build can be installed side by side

For more answers, see the [FAQs](/content/faqs).

# Universal App Configuration

Configure your universal app's appearance, behavior, and security settings through `config/config.json`.

---

## App Name

Set the display name that appears in device launchers, app stores, and system settings.

### Configuration

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "appId": "com.yourcompany.myapp",
    "appName": "My Awesome App"
  }
}
```

`appName` is used on both platforms. `appId` is the Android application id and the iOS bundle id; see [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment#configure-the-app).

### Platform-Specific Names

Without a top-level `appName`, each platform reads its own:

```json
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "android": {
      "appName": "MyApp for Android"
    },
    "ios": {
      "appName": "MyApp for iOS"
    }
  }
}
```

---

## App Icon

The simplest icon is one file: `public/icon.png`, a square PNG of at least 1024x1024 pixels with no transparency. Catalyst turns it into the Android launcher icons and a single 1024 iOS AppIcon. New apps start with a placeholder there. To control each size yourself, use the folders below; they take precedence over `public/icon.png`.

### Android Icons

Place density-specific icons in `public/android/appIcons/`:

| Density | Filename | Size (px) |
|---------|----------|-----------|
| `mdpi` | `icon-mdpi.png` | 48 x 48 |
| `hdpi` | `icon-hdpi.png` | 72 x 72 |
| `xhdpi` | `icon-xhdpi.png` | 96 x 96 |
| `xxhdpi` | `icon-xxhdpi.png` | 144 x 144 |
| `xxxhdpi` | `icon-xxxhdpi.png` | 192 x 192 |

**Supported formats:** PNG, JPG, JPEG

**Behavior:**
- Automatically applied during build
- Missing densities use nearest available resource
- Falls back to `public/icon.png`, then to the default Catalyst icon

### iOS Icons

Place icons in `public/ios/appIcons/` following the pattern: `icon-{size}-{scale}.{ext}`

| Filename | Size (px) | Purpose |
|----------|-----------|---------|
| icon-20x20-2x.png | 40×40 | iPhone Notification |
| icon-20x20-3x.png | 60×60 | iPhone Notification |
| icon-29x29-2x.png | 58×58 | iPhone Settings |
| icon-29x29-3x.png | 87×87 | iPhone Settings |
| icon-40x40-2x.png | 80×80 | iPhone Spotlight |
| icon-40x40-3x.png | 120×120 | iPhone Spotlight |
| icon-60x60-2x.png | 120×120 | iPhone App |
| icon-60x60-3x.png | 180×180 | iPhone App |
| icon-1024x1024-1x.png | 1024×1024 | App Store |

**Supported formats:** PNG, JPG, JPEG

### File Structure

```
your-project/
├── public/
│   ├── android/appIcons/
│   │   ├── icon-mdpi.png
│   │   ├── icon-hdpi.png
│   │   ├── icon-xhdpi.png
│   │   ├── icon-xxhdpi.png
│   │   └── icon-xxxhdpi.png
│   └── ios/appIcons/
│       ├── icon-20x20-2x.png
│       ├── icon-20x20-3x.png
│       ├── icon-29x29-2x.png
│       ├── icon-29x29-3x.png
│       ├── icon-40x40-2x.png
│       ├── icon-40x40-3x.png
│       ├── icon-60x60-2x.png
│       ├── icon-60x60-3x.png
│       └── icon-1024x1024-1x.png
```

---

## Splashscreen

Configure a custom splashscreen displayed during app startup.

### Configuration

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "splashScreen": {
      "duration": 2000,
      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff",
      "imageWidth": 120,
      "imageHeight": 120,
      "cornerRadius": 20
    }
  }
}
```

### Options

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `duration` | number | `1000` | Display time in milliseconds. Ignored when an HTML splash is used |
| `minDuration` | number | `0` | Minimum time in milliseconds the HTML splash stays on screen |
| `backgroundColor` | string | `"#ffffff"` | Background color (hex) |
| `imageWidth` | number | `120` | Image width in dp/px |
| `imageHeight` | number | `120` | Image height in dp/px |
| `cornerRadius` | number | `20` | Corner radius (0 for square) |

### Custom Images

**Android:** Place image at `public/android/splashscreen.{png|jpg|webp}`
- Supported: PNG, JPG, WebP
- Fallback: App launcher icon

**iOS:** Place image at `public/ios/splashscreen.{png|jpg|jpeg}`
- Recommended: PNG, 512x512px
- File size: Under 1MB
- Fallback: Progress bar with loader

### HTML Splash

To show an animation while the app loads, add `public/splashscreen.html`. It goes at the root of `public/`, not in `public/android` or `public/ios`, and both platforms use the same file. It only takes effect when `splashScreen` is set in the config.

On launch the app shows the native splash image, then the HTML splash, and then the app once its first page has loaded. Set `minDuration` to keep the animation on screen for at least that many milliseconds, even when the page loads sooner. If the page takes longer than 10 seconds, the HTML splash is dismissed anyway. `duration` is ignored in this mode. New apps ship an HTML splash with `minDuration` set to `7000` so its animation can finish. Lower it for a shorter splash, or set it to `0` to dismiss the splash as soon as the page loads.

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "splashScreen": {
      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff",
      "minDuration": 1200
    }
  }
}
```

The file has a few rules:

- Keep it to one self-contained file. Put CSS and JavaScript inline and embed images as `data:` URIs.
- Paint your own opaque, full-screen background. The native image sits underneath.
- Do not make network requests. Android blocks them.
- The page has no access to the native bridge.
- Prefer CSS `transform` and `opacity` animations. The splash runs while the app is loading, so heavy JavaScript competes with it.

The native build tells the page which colour the native splash uses. Both platforms add a script at the start of `<head>` that sets `window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__` to `{ backgroundColor: "#rrggbb" }`, taken from `splashScreen.backgroundColor`, or white when that is not set. Paint the page with it so the native layer and the page read as one surface. The value is only set for a six-digit hex colour. For any other value, and when you open the file in a browser, `window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__` is undefined, so keep a fallback colour in your CSS.

```js
var cfg = window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__
if (cfg && cfg.backgroundColor) {
  document.documentElement.style.background = cfg.backgroundColor
}
```

```html title="public/splashscreen.html"
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
    <style>
      html, body { margin: 0; height: 100%; background: #ffffff; }
      body { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; }
      .dot {
        width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 50%; background: #3b5bdb;
        animation: pulse 1s ease-in-out infinite alternate;
      }
      @keyframes pulse {
        from { transform: scale(0.6); opacity: 0.4; }
        to { transform: scale(1); opacity: 1; }
      }
    </style>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div class="dot"></div>
  </body>
</html>
```

Delete the file to go back to the image-only splash.

### Examples

#### Basic Splashscreen

```json
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "splashScreen": {
      "duration": 2000,
      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff"
    }
  }
}
```

#### Circular Icon

```json
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "splashScreen": {
      "duration": 2000,
      "backgroundColor": "#1a1a1a",
      "imageWidth": 150,
      "imageHeight": 150,
      "cornerRadius": 75
    }
  }
}
```

#### Auto-Dismiss (iOS Only)

```json
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "splashScreen": {
      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff"
    }
  }
}
```

Omitting `duration` on iOS auto-dismisses when WebView loads.

### Platform Differences

**iOS:**
- Auto-dismiss when `duration` is omitted
- Smooth fade-out animation

**Android:**
- Theme support (adapts to light/dark mode)

### Best Practices

| App Load Time | Recommendation |
|---------------|----------------|
| < 1 second | Auto-dismiss (iOS) or 1000ms |
| 1-3 seconds | 2000-3000ms |
| > 3 seconds | Auto-dismiss (iOS) or 3000ms |

---

## Performance Profiler

Enable the Catalyst Profiler for a debug build:

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "profiler": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

Use [Performance Profiling](/content/Core%20Concepts/performance-profiling) for the Android Chrome DevTools workflow, iOS trace export, captured signals, and the `window.CatalystPerf` API.

The profiler is disabled by default and only runs in debug builds. Rebuild the native app after changing the setting.

---

## Edge-to-Edge

Let the WebView draw behind the status bar and navigation bar.

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "edgeToEdge": {
      "enabled": true,
      "statusBarStyle": "auto"
    }
  }
}
```

### Options

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `enabled` | boolean | `false` | Draw page content behind the system bars on Android and iOS |
| `statusBarStyle` | string | `"auto"` | System bar icon colour. Android only for now |

`statusBarStyle` accepts these values:

- `auto` follows the system light or dark theme.
- `dark-content` uses dark icons, for light pages.
- `light-content` uses light icons, for dark pages.

When edge-to-edge is enabled, the app is responsible for keeping content clear of the system bars. Read the insets with [`useSafeArea()`](/content/API%20Reference/hooks#usesafearea) and apply them as padding. The values are in CSS pixels on both platforms. On Android they also update when the insets change, for example when the user switches navigation mode. When edge-to-edge is disabled, the insets are `0`.

On iOS the WebView does not pad the page itself, the same as on Android, so the page draws under the status bar and the home indicator until it applies the insets. Before 1.2.1, iOS added the safe-area padding on its own.

On Android 10 (API 29) and later the system bars are fully transparent. Below API 29 the navigation bar keeps a translucent scrim.

---

## Whitelisting

Control network access and navigation through URL whitelisting.

### Configuration

```json title="config/config.json"
{
  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
    "accessControl": {
      "enabled": true,
      "allowedUrls": [
        "https://api.example.com/*",
        "*.example.com",
        "https://cdn.example.com/assets/*"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

### Options

| Property | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `enabled` | boolean | `false` | Enable URL whitelisting |
| `allowedUrls` | string[] | `[]` | Permitted URL patterns |

**Behavior:**
- `enabled: true` - Only whitelisted URLs accessible (default deny)
- `enabled: false` - All URLs accessible (no restrictions)

### URL Patterns

#### Exact Match

```json
{
  "allowedUrls": [
    "https://api.example.com/users",
    "https://cdn.example.com/logo.png"
  ]
}
```

#### Wildcard Match

```json
{
  "allowedUrls": [
    "https://api.example.com/*",
    "https://*.example.com/api/*"
  ]
}
```

#### Subdomain Match

```json
{
  "allowedUrls": [
    "*.example.com",
    "*.cdn.example.com"
  ]
}
```

### Examples

#### API Endpoints

```json
{
  "accessControl": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowedUrls": [
      "https://api.myapp.com/auth/*",
      "https://api.myapp.com/users/*",
      "https://api.myapp.com/data/*"
    ]
  }
}
```

#### CDN Resources

```json
{
  "accessControl": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowedUrls": [
      "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/*",
      "*.cloudfront.net"
    ]
  }
}
```

#### Third-Party Services

```json
{
  "accessControl": {
    "enabled": true,
    "allowedUrls": [
      "https://maps.googleapis.com/*",
      "https://api.stripe.com/*",
      "*.analytics.google.com"
    ]
  }
}
```

### How It Works

1. All network requests blocked by default when enabled
2. External links open in system browser
3. URLs matched against patterns in order
4. First matching pattern allows the request
5. No match = request blocked

### Security Benefits

- **Default deny** - Secure baseline blocks all unknown requests
- **Explicit allow** - Only whitelisted URLs accessible
- **Navigation control** - External links handled by system browser

---

## Protocol Configuration

A release build loads `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`, and its scheme decides the protocol. Use `https://` for store builds; plain `http://` builds with a warning. Debug builds load the dev server over HTTP, or `LOCAL_IP` when it is a real host.

7	# Universal App
8	
9	A Universal App in Catalyst is a single React application that runs as:
10	
11	- a server-rendered web app
12	- an Android app (native webview host)
13	- an iOS app (native webview host)

15	The philosophy is simple: keep product logic shared, while allowing platform-specific behavior only where it adds user value.

17	## How It Works
18	
19	In Catalyst, a universal app is still a web app at its core:
20	
21	- the UI is the same React application used on the web
22	- the app still follows the SSR and hydration model
23	- a native WebView container hosts that app on Android and iOS
24	- native features are exposed through `WebBridge` and framework hooks
25	
26	The result is a web-first architecture with native delivery and native capabilities when required.
27	
28	## Design Principles
29	
30	- **Shared-first**: Write features once; avoid forked product logic.
31	- **Performance-first**: SSR for web, optimized startup for native shells.
32	- **Progressive native**: Add native capabilities through hooks when needed.

162	# Running Universal Apps
163	
164	## Prerequisites
165	
166	- Node.js and npm
167	- For iOS: macOS with Xcode installed (it never needs to be opened)
168	- For Android: nothing else; Android Studio is optional
169	
170	---
171	
172	## Run the app
173	
174	```bash
175	npm run android
176	npm run ios
177	```
178	
179	Each run:
180	
181	1. Checks the toolchain and installs what is missing, after asking. See [Android Emulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/android-emulator-setup) and [iOS Simulator Setup](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/ios-emulator-setup) for what that covers.
182	2. Picks where to run: the emulator or simulator, or a connected phone.
183	3. Starts the dev server with `catalyst start` when nothing answers on `NODE_SERVER_PORT`, and waits until it answers. The server keeps running after the build, with its output in a log file whose path is printed. A dev server you started yourself is reused.
184	4. Builds, installs and opens the app. Edit your code and the dev server reloads it.
185	
186	On Android, each run also saves the app as an APK in `build-output/android/debug/`. See [Share a test build](#share-a-test-build).
187	
188	Apps created before Catalyst 1.2.0 have `buildApp:android` and `buildApp:ios` scripts, which run the same commands. To get the short names, add these scripts to `package.json`:
189	
190	```json title="package.json"
191	{
192	  "scripts": {
193	    "android": "catalyst buildApp:android",
194	    "ios": "catalyst buildApp:ios",
195	    "android:release": "catalyst buildApp:android --release",
196	    "ios:release": "catalyst buildApp:ios --release"
197	  }
198	}
199	```
200	
201	---
202	
203	## Emulator, simulator or phone
204	
205	The app runs on the Android emulator or the iOS simulator by default. When a phone is connected and you run the command in a terminal, it asks which one to use. Your pick is remembered for this machine in `.catalyst/local.json`, which is kept out of git, and offered as the default next time.
206	
207	To go straight to the phone, pass `--device`:
208	
209	```bash
210	npm run android -- --device
211	npm run ios -- --device
212	```
213	
214	- Android: turn on USB debugging in Developer options and accept the "Allow USB debugging" prompt on the phone. With several phones connected and no terminal, set `ANDROID_SERIAL` to the serial `adb devices` shows.
215	- iPhone: connect it, unlock it, accept "Trust This Computer" and turn on Developer Mode (Settings > Privacy & Security). With several iPhones connected and no terminal, set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios.deviceUDID`.
216	
217	Without a terminal and without `--device`, the app always runs on the emulator or simulator.
218	
219	---
220	
221	## How the app reaches the dev server
222	
223	A debug build loads the dev server, never `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`. Catalyst works out the address for each target and puts it into the build only; `config/config.json` is not changed.
224	
225	The one exception is `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP`. When it is a real host, such as your public site or a staging server on your VPN or office network, a debug build loads that host instead, with `port` and `useHttps`, and prints a line saying so. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0` and this computer's own addresses mean the dev server.
226	
227	- Android emulator and USB phone: the app loads `http://localhost:<port>`. After the install and before the launch, Catalyst runs `adb reverse` for `NODE_SERVER_PORT`, the Vite HMR port (24678, or `devServer.hmr.port` from `buildConfig.js`) and every `localhost:<port>` in `config/config.json`, such as `API_URL`. A USB phone needs no Wi-Fi for this.
228	- iOS simulator: it shares the Mac's network, so the app loads `http://localhost:<port>`.
229	- iPhone: the app loads the dev server from the Mac's Bonjour name, `<Local Hostname>.local` (System Settings > General > Sharing), or the Mac's LAN IP when it has no Local Hostname. The iPhone and the Mac must be on the same Wi-Fi. Catalyst starts the dev server listening on the network for this. If a dev server is already running for this Mac only, the build stops with [NATIVE-006](https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/NATIVE/NATIVE-006.md): stop that server and run the build again.
230	
231	A debug build also adds the dev server's address to `accessControl.allowedUrls`, and points an `apiBaseUrl` on localhost or on your production `url` at the dev server.
232	
233	### Run on a physical iPhone
234	
235	An iPhone build is signed, even in debug. It signs with what `config/config.json` sets and looks nothing up on its own.
236	
237	Set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios.developmentTeam` to your 10-character Apple team ID. With a paid account it is under Membership details at developer.apple.com/account. With a free account, open any Xcode project, choose your Personal Team under Signing & Capabilities, and copy `DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` from Build Settings. With Xcode signed in to that team (Xcode > Settings > Accounts), Xcode signs automatically: it creates the development certificate and profile and registers the iPhone.
238	
239	To sign with a development profile you already installed, also set `ios.provisioningProfile` to its name. The profile must include this iPhone and match the app's bundle ID, and its certificate must be in your keychain. Set `ios.bundleIdentifier` when the profile is for a different ID than `appId`.
240	
241	```json title="config/config.json"
242	{
243	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
244	    "ios": {
245	      "bundleIdentifier": "com.acme.shop",
246	      "developmentTeam": "ABCDE12345",
247	      "provisioningProfile": "Acme Shop Development"
248	    }
249	  }
250	}
251	```
252	
253	When Xcode cannot sign it, the build stops with [IOS-010](https://github.com/tata1mg/catalyst-core/blob/main/errors/IOS/IOS-010.md), which includes Xcode's line saying why. With a free account, the first install also needs you to trust the developer on the iPhone (Settings > General > VPN & Device Management), and the app stops opening after seven days until you build it again.
254	
255	macOS Keychain may ask for your login password while the build signs the app. Choose Always Allow so later builds do not ask again.
256	
257	The iPhone must be on the same Wi-Fi as the Mac, and the app needs Local Network access to reach the dev server. Allow it when iOS asks the first time the app opens, or turn it on later in Settings > Privacy & Security > Local Network.
258	
259	### Upgrading from an older setup
260	
261	Before Catalyst 1.2.0, the emulator setup wrote your LAN address into `config/config.json`. The first debug build on 1.2.0 puts `localhost` back where that address was saved: any value equal to one of this machine's current IP addresses (such as `LOCAL_IP`, `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` or `PUBLIC_STATIC_ASSET_URL`), and any `http://` URL on one of those addresses. A private `LOCAL_IP` that `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` also holds counts as a saved address too, even when this machine now has a different one, for example on another Wi-Fi network. It prints each change. Other addresses, such as `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1`, a container's IP or a staging server on your network, are left as they are, and so is `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`. It runs once per checkout and records that in `.catalyst/local.json`. It never runs for a release build or when `CI` is set, and apps with `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.allowPrivateHost` set to `true` are left alone. Review the change and commit it. If this checkout already ran a 1.2.0 debug build, for example a canary, the rewrite will not run again: set `LOCAL_IP` and `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME` to `localhost` by hand as shown below.
262	
263	#### Fix a stale LAN address by hand
264	
265	When `npm run start` cannot bind `NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME`, or the app cannot reach the dev server after your IP address changed, the config still holds an address this machine no longer has. Set both keys to `localhost`:
266	
267	```json title="config/config.json"
268	{
269	  "NODE_SERVER_HOSTNAME": "localhost",
270	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
271	    "LOCAL_IP": "localhost"
272	  }
273	}
274	```
275	
276	Debug builds then work out how the emulator, simulator or phone reaches the dev server. If you run the dev server yourself for a phone on the same Wi-Fi, use this machine's current IP address for both keys instead, and update it when the address changes. Change any `PUBLIC_STATIC_ASSET_URL` or `API_URL` on the old address the same way.
277

280	## Set the app icon
281	
282	Replace the placeholder `public/icon.png` with a square PNG of at least 1024x1024 pixels. Android uses it as the launcher icon and iOS as a single 1024 AppIcon that Xcode scales. Keep it opaque; the App Store rejects icons with transparency. Per-density icons in `public/android/appIcons` and sized icons in `public/ios/appIcons` take precedence when present.
283

285	
286	## Share a test build
287	
288	Every `npm run android` saves the app it installed in `build-output/android/debug/`. `<App>` is your app name, and the next run overwrites the file:
289	
290	- `<App>-debug.apk` when the app loads a real host from `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP`. It works on any Android phone that can reach that host.
291	- `<App>-debug-devserver.apk` when the app loads this computer's dev server. It only works while that dev server runs, so it is not one to share.
292	
293	These are test builds: they can be debugged and allow plain HTTP, so never upload them to a store. `build-output/` has its own `.gitignore`, so the files stay out of git.
294	
295	To share a test build with someone:
296	
297	1. Set `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.LOCAL_IP` to your site, for example a public staging site or one on your VPN, with `port` and `useHttps` to match.
298	2. Run `npm run android` (`npm run buildApp:android` in apps created before 1.2.0).
299	3. Send them `build-output/android/debug/<App>-debug.apk`. They open it on the phone and allow the install.
300	
301	Or build the release with `npm run android:release` and share the `<App>.apk` it writes next to the AAB. That APK loads your production `url`. It will not install over a copy from Google Play, so uninstall that first.
302

305	## Build for release
306	
307	```bash
308	npm run android:release
309	npm run ios:release
310	```
311	
312	In apps created before 1.2.0, run `npm run buildApp:android -- --release` and `npm run buildApp:ios -- --release`.
313	
314	A release build loads `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url` and refuses a local or private host. Run in a terminal, it asks once for an app id or website that is missing or still a placeholder, and saves your answer to `config/config.json`. [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment) covers signing, version numbers and CI. `buildType: "release"` in `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.android` or `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios` still builds a release, with a deprecation warning; use the release scripts instead and set `buildType` back to `debug` or remove it.

358	## App Name
359	
360	Set the display name that appears in device launchers, app stores, and system settings.
361	
362	### Configuration
363	
364	```json title="config/config.json"
365	{
366	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
367	    "appId": "com.yourcompany.myapp",
368	    "appName": "My Awesome App"
369	  }
370	}
371	```
372	
373	`appName` is used on both platforms. `appId` is the Android application id and the iOS bundle id; see [Universal App Deployment](/content/Deployment/universal-app-deployment#configure-the-app).
374	
375	### Platform-Specific Names
376	
377	Without a top-level `appName`, each platform reads its own:
378	
379	```json
380	{
381	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
382	    "android": {
383	      "appName": "MyApp for Android"
384	    },
385	    "ios": {
386	      "appName": "MyApp for iOS"
387	    }
388	  }
389	}
390	```

394	## App Icon
395	
396	The simplest icon is one file: `public/icon.png`, a square PNG of at least 1024x1024 pixels with no transparency. Catalyst turns it into the Android launcher icons and a single 1024 iOS AppIcon. New apps start with a placeholder there. To control each size yourself, use the folders below; they take precedence over `public/icon.png`.
397	
398	### Android Icons
399	
400	Place density-specific icons in `public/android/appIcons/`:
401	
402	| Density | Filename | Size (px) |
403	|---------|----------|-----------|
404	| `mdpi` | `icon-mdpi.png` | 48 x 48 |
405	| `hdpi` | `icon-hdpi.png` | 72 x 72 |
406	| `xhdpi` | `icon-xhdpi.png` | 96 x 96 |
407	| `xxhdpi` | `icon-xxhdpi.png` | 144 x 144 |
408	| `xxxhdpi` | `icon-xxxhdpi.png` | 192 x 192 |
409	
410	**Supported formats:** PNG, JPG, JPEG
411	
412	**Behavior:**
413	- Automatically applied during build
414	- Missing densities use nearest available resource
415	- Falls back to `public/icon.png`, then to the default Catalyst icon
416	
417	### iOS Icons
418	
419	Place icons in `public/ios/appIcons/` following the pattern: `icon-{size}-{scale}.{ext}`
420	
421	| Filename | Size (px) | Purpose |
422	|----------|-----------|---------|
423	| icon-20x20-2x.png | 40×40 | iPhone Notification |
424	| icon-20x20-3x.png | 60×60 | iPhone Notification |
425	| icon-29x29-2x.png | 58×58 | iPhone Settings |
426	| icon-29x29-3x.png | 87×87 | iPhone Settings |
427	| icon-40x40-2x.png | 80×80 | iPhone Spotlight |
428	| icon-40x40-3x.png | 120×120 | iPhone Spotlight |
429	| icon-60x60-2x.png | 120×120 | iPhone App |
430	| icon-60x60-3x.png | 180×180 | iPhone App |
431	| icon-1024x1024-1x.png | 1024×1024 | App Store |
432	
433	**Supported formats:** PNG, JPG, JPEG
434	
435	### File Structure
436	
437	```
438	your-project/
439	├── public/
440	│   ├── android/appIcons/
441	│   │   ├── icon-mdpi.png
442	│   │   ├── icon-hdpi.png
443	│   │   ├── icon-xhdpi.png
444	│   │   ├── icon-xxhdpi.png
445	│   │   └── icon-xxxhdpi.png
446	│   └── ios/appIcons/
447	│       ├── icon-20x20-2x.png
448	│       ├── icon-20x20-3x.png
449	│       ├── icon-29x29-2x.png
450	│       ├── icon-29x29-3x.png
451	│       ├── icon-40x40-2x.png

456	```

460	## Splashscreen
461	
462	Configure a custom splashscreen displayed during app startup.
463	
464	### Configuration
465	
466	```json title="config/config.json"
467	{
468	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
469	    "splashScreen": {
470	      "duration": 2000,
471	      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff",
472	      "imageWidth": 120,
473	      "imageHeight": 120,
474	      "cornerRadius": 20
475	    }
476	  }
477	}
478	```
479	
480	### Options
481	
482	| Property | Type | Default | Description |
483	|----------|------|---------|-------------|
484	| `duration` | number | `1000` | Display time in milliseconds. Ignored when an HTML splash is used |
485	| `minDuration` | number | `0` | Minimum time in milliseconds the HTML splash stays on screen |
486	| `backgroundColor` | string | `"#ffffff"` | Background color (hex) |
487	| `imageWidth` | number | `120` | Image width in dp/px |
488	| `imageHeight` | number | `120` | Image height in dp/px |
489	| `cornerRadius` | number | `20` | Corner radius (0 for square) |
490	
491	### Custom Images
492	
493	**Android:** Place image at `public/android/splashscreen.{png|jpg|webp}`
494	- Supported: PNG, JPG, WebP
495	- Fallback: App launcher icon
496	
497	**iOS:** Place image at `public/ios/splashscreen.{png|jpg|jpeg}`
498	- Recommended: PNG, 512x512px
499	- File size: Under 1MB
500	- Fallback: Progress bar with loader
501	
502	### HTML Splash
503	
504	To show an animation while the app loads, add `public/splashscreen.html`. It goes at the root of `public/`, not in `public/android` or `public/ios`, and both platforms use the same file. It only takes effect when `splashScreen` is set in the config.
505	
506	On launch the app shows the native splash image, then the HTML splash, and then the app once its first page has loaded. Set `minDuration` to keep the animation on screen for at least that many milliseconds, even when the page loads sooner. If the page takes longer than 10 seconds, the HTML splash is dismissed anyway. `duration` is ignored in this mode. New apps ship an HTML splash with `minDuration` set to `7000` so its animation can finish. Lower it for a shorter splash, or set it to `0` to dismiss the splash as soon as the page loads.
507	
508	```json title="config/config.json"
509	{
510	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
511	    "splashScreen": {
512	      "backgroundColor": "#ffffff",
513	      "minDuration": 1200
514	    }
515	  }
516	}
517	```
518	
519	The file has a few rules:
520	
521	- Keep it to one self-contained file. Put CSS and JavaScript inline and embed images as `data:` URIs.
522	- Paint your own opaque, full-screen background. The native image sits underneath.
523	- Do not make network requests. Android blocks them.
524	- The page has no access to the native bridge.
525	- Prefer CSS `transform` and `opacity` animations. The splash runs while the app is loading, so heavy JavaScript competes with it.
526	
527	The native build tells the page which colour the native splash uses. Both platforms add a script at the start of `<head>` that sets `window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__` to `{ backgroundColor: "#rrggbb" }`, taken from `splashScreen.backgroundColor`, or white when that is not set. Paint the page with it so the native layer and the page read as one surface. The value is only set for a six-digit hex colour. For any other value, and when you open the file in a browser, `window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__` is undefined, so keep a fallback colour in your CSS.
528	
529	```js
530	var cfg = window.__CATALYST_SPLASH__
531	if (cfg && cfg.backgroundColor) {
532	  document.documentElement.style.background = cfg.backgroundColor
533	}
534	```
535	
536	```html title="public/splashscreen.html"
537	<!doctype html>
538	<html>
539	  <head>
540	    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
541	    <style>
542	      html, body { margin: 0; height: 100%; background: #ffffff; }
543	      body { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; }
544	      .dot {
545	        width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 50%; background: #3b5bdb;
546	        animation: pulse 1s ease-in-out infinite alternate;
547	      }
548	      @keyframes pulse {
549	        from { transform: scale(0.6); opacity: 0.4; }
550	        to { transform: scale(1); opacity: 1; }
551	      }
552	    </style>
553	  </head>
554	  <body>
555	    <div class="dot"></div>
556	  </body>
557	</html>
558	```
559	
560	Delete the file to go back to the image-only splash.
561

646	## Edge-to-Edge
647	
648	Let the WebView draw behind the status bar and navigation bar.
649	
650	```json title="config/config.json"
651	{
652	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
653	    "edgeToEdge": {
654	      "enabled": true,
655	      "statusBarStyle": "auto"
656	    }
657	  }
658	}
659	```
660	
661	### Options
662	
663	| Property | Type | Default | Description |
664	|----------|------|---------|-------------|
665	| `enabled` | boolean | `false` | Draw page content behind the system bars on Android and iOS |
666	| `statusBarStyle` | string | `"auto"` | System bar icon colour. Android only for now |
667	
668	`statusBarStyle` accepts these values:
669	
670	- `auto` follows the system light or dark theme.
671	- `dark-content` uses dark icons, for light pages.
672	- `light-content` uses light icons, for dark pages.
673	
674	When edge-to-edge is enabled, the app is responsible for keeping content clear of the system bars. Read the insets with [`useSafeArea()`](/content/API%20Reference/hooks#usesafearea) and apply them as padding. The values are in CSS pixels on both platforms. On Android they also update when the insets change, for example when the user switches navigation mode. When edge-to-edge is disabled, the insets are `0`.
675	
676	On iOS the WebView does not pad the page itself, the same as on Android, so the page draws under the status bar and the home indicator until it applies the insets. Before 1.2.1, iOS added the safe-area padding on its own.
677	
678	On Android 10 (API 29) and later the system bars are fully transparent. Below API 29 the navigation bar keeps a translucent scrim.
679

682	## Whitelisting
683	
684	Control network access and navigation through URL whitelisting.
685	
686	### Configuration
687	
688	```json title="config/config.json"
689	{
690	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
691	    "accessControl": {
692	      "enabled": true,
693	      "allowedUrls": [
694	        "https://api.example.com/*",
695	        "*.example.com",
696	        "https://cdn.example.com/assets/*"
697	      ]
698	    }
699	  }
700	}
701	```
702	
703	### Options
704	
705	| Property | Type | Default | Description |
706	|----------|------|---------|-------------|
707	| `enabled` | boolean | `false` | Enable URL whitelisting |
708	| `allowedUrls` | string[] | `[]` | Permitted URL patterns |
709	
710	**Behavior:**
711	- `enabled: true` - Only whitelisted URLs accessible (default deny)
712	- `enabled: false` - All URLs accessible (no restrictions)
713	
714	### URL Patterns
715	
716	#### Exact Match
717	
718	```json
719	{
720	  "allowedUrls": [
721	    "https://api.example.com/users",
722	    "https://cdn.example.com/logo.png"
723	  ]
724	}
725	```
726	
727	#### Wildcard Match
728	
729	```json
730	{
731	  "allowedUrls": [
732	    "https://api.example.com/*",
733	    "https://*.example.com/api/*"
734	  ]
735	}
736	```
737	
738	#### Subdomain Match
739	
740	```json
741	{
742	  "allowedUrls": [
743	    "*.example.com",
744	    "*.cdn.example.com"
745	  ]
746	}
747	```
748	
749	### Examples
750	
751	#### API Endpoints
752	
753	```json
754	{
755	  "accessControl": {
756	    "enabled": true,
757	    "allowedUrls": [
758	      "https://api.myapp.com/auth/*",
759	      "https://api.myapp.com/users/*",
760	      "https://api.myapp.com/data/*"
761	    ]
762	  }
763	}
764	```
765	
766	#### CDN Resources
767	
768	```json
769	{
770	  "accessControl": {
771	    "enabled": true,
772	    "allowedUrls": [
773	      "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/*",
774	      "*.cloudfront.net"
775	    ]
776	  }
777	}
778	```
779	
780	#### Third-Party Services
781	
782	```json
783	{
784	  "accessControl": {
785	    "enabled": true,
786	    "allowedUrls": [
787	      "https://maps.googleapis.com/*",
788	      "https://api.stripe.com/*",
789	      "*.analytics.google.com"
790	    ]
791	  }
792	}
793	```
794	
795	### How It Works
796	
797	1. All network requests blocked by default when enabled
798	2. External links open in system browser
799	3. URLs matched against patterns in order
800	4. First matching pattern allows the request
801	5. No match = request blocked
802	
803	### Security Benefits
804	
805	- **Default deny** - Secure baseline blocks all unknown requests
806	- **Explicit allow** - Only whitelisted URLs accessible
807	- **Navigation control** - External links handled by system browser
808	
809	---
810	
811	## Protocol Configuration
812	
813	A release build loads `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.url`, and its scheme decides the protocol. Use `https://` for store builds; plain `http://` builds with a warning. Debug builds load the dev server over HTTP, or `LOCAL_IP` when it is a real host.
814	
815	```json title="config/config.json"
816	{
817	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
818	    "url": "https://www.myapp.com",
819	    "accessControl": {
820	      "enabled": true,
821	      "allowedUrls": ["https://api.myapp.com/*"]
822	    }
823	  }
824	}
825	```
826	
827	Apps without `url` still use `useHttps` (default `false`) with `LOCAL_IP` and `port` for the release host.
828	
829	---
830	
831	## Complete Configuration Example
832	
833	<ConfigExample type="universalAppConfig" />
834	
835	---
836	
837	## Configuration Tips
838	
839	1. **App Names** - Keep under 30 characters for best display
840	2. **Icons** - Provide all required sizes for professional appearance
841	3. **Splashscreen** - Match duration to actual load time
842	4. **Whitelisting** - Start with minimal URLs, add as needed
843	5. **Protocol** - Always use HTTPS in production
844	6. **Testing** - Test configuration on both platforms before release
845	7. **Release Builds** - Use `npm run android:release` and `npm run ios:release`; `buildType: "release"` is deprecated
846	
847	---
848	
849	## See Also
850	
851	- [Running Universal Apps](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Universal%20App/RunUniversalApp) - Build and run commands
852	- [Hooks](/content/API%20Reference/hooks) - Device capabilities
853	- [Build Optimization](/content/14-Best%20Practices/08-Android-Build-Optimization.md) - Performance tuning
854	- [Cache Management](/content/Guides%20and%20Tutorials/First%20Universal%20App/Cache-Management) - Cache configuration
855	# Offline Support
856	
857	## What it does
858	- Shows a friendly offline page when the device has no connectivity.
859	- Lets that page trigger a native retry so users can get back to their last intended page once they reconnect.
860	- Surfaces connectivity signals to your web code via a React hook, so you can adapt UI (banners, pause live data, etc.) while native handles the fallback view.
861	
862	## How to set it up
863	- Add `public/offline.html` to your web app. Keep it self contained (avoid external assets or API calls) and lightweight.
864	- Add a clear “Retry” control that links to `catalyst://retry`. Both Android and iOS listen for this and will reload the last target URL if the device is online; if still offline they keep the offline page visible.
865	- Use the page to explain what users should do (“Check connection, then tap Retry”), and keep styling minimal so it loads instantly from the bundle.
866	
867	## How native uses it (high level)
868	- Build time: the native build copies `public/offline.html` into each app bundle. If the file is missing, no fallback is bundled.
869	- Launch path: before the first request (including app open and notification taps), both platforms check connectivity. If offline, they render your bundled offline page instead of hitting the network.
870	- Retry flow: when your offline page opens `catalyst://retry`, native checks connectivity and reloads the last intended URL if back online.
871	
872	## Hook for live status: `useNetworkStatus()`
873	- Purpose: simple React hook that reports connectivity from the native bridge: `{ online: boolean, type: 'wifi'|'cellular'|...|null, error }`.
874	- Why use it: drive in-app banners, pause/resume live data, or disable actions while offline—while native still owns the full-screen offline fallback.
875	- Example:
876	  ```jsx
877	  import { useNetworkStatus } from "catalyst-core/hooks"
878	
879	  export function ConnectivityBanner() {
880	      const { online, type } = useNetworkStatus()
881	      if (online) return null
882	      return <div>Offline{type ? ` (${type})` : ""}. Reconnect and tap Retry.</div>
883	  }
884	  ```
885	
886	## Quick verification
887	- With `public/offline.html` present, launch the app in airplane mode: you should see your offline page immediately.
888	- While on the offline page, re-enable network and tap your `catalyst://retry` control: it should reload the last intended URL.
889	- In your React code, log `useNetworkStatus()` and toggle airplane mode to confirm you receive connectivity updates.
890	# Universal App Cache Management
891	
892	## Overview
893	The cache manager implementation provides efficient caching mechanisms for web resources in both Android and iOS WebView applications. It supports configurable caching patterns, revalidation strategies, and automatic cache cleanup.
894	
895	## Configuration
896	
897	### Android Configuration
898	Configure caching through the `config.json` file:
899	
900	```json
901	{
902	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
903	    "android": {
904	      "cachePattern": "*.css,*.js"
905	    }
906	  }
907	}
908	```
909	
910	Configuration options:
911	- `cachePattern`: Comma-separated list of file patterns to cache (e.g., "*.css,*.js")
912	
913	The command decides the build type, not the config: `npm run android` makes a debug build for development with Hot Module Replacement (HMR), and `npm run android:release` makes the release build. `buildType` in `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.android` is deprecated.
914	
915	### iOS Configuration
916	Configure caching through `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios.cachePattern`:
917	
918	```json
919	{
920	  "WEBVIEW_CONFIG": {
921	    "ios": {
922	      "cachePattern": ["*.css", "*.js"]
923	    }
924	  }
925	}
926	```
927	
928	Configuration options:
929	- `cachePattern`: An array of file patterns to cache (e.g., `["*.css", "*.js"]`). A single string is read as one pattern, not split on commas.
930	
931	`npm run ios` makes a debug build for development, and `npm run ios:release` makes the release build. `buildType` in `WEBVIEW_CONFIG.ios` is deprecated.
932	
933	## Cache Pattern Format
934	
935	Both platforms support wildcard patterns for cache matching:
936	- `*.css`: Matches all CSS files
937	- `*.js`: Matches all JavaScript files
938	- Multiple patterns go in one comma-separated string on Android, and in an array on iOS
939	- File extensions are case-insensitive
940	
941	## Internal Implementation
942	
943	### Android Cache Manager
944	
945	The Android implementation features:
946	
947	1. Two-Level Caching:
948	   - Memory cache using LruCache for fast access
949	   - Disk cache for persistence
950	   
951	2. Cache Entry Management:
952	   - Cache entries include:
953	     - Response data
954	     - Timestamp
955	     - ETag
956	     - Last-Modified headers
957	
958	3. Cache Validation Strategy:
959	   - Implements stale-while-revalidate pattern
960	   - Handles cache expiration
961	   - Supports background revalidation
962	
963	4. Automatic Cache Maintenance:
964	   - Maximum cache size: 100MB
965	   - Automatic cleanup of expired entries
966	   - LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy
967	
968	### iOS Cache Manager
969	
970	The iOS implementation uses a custom URL protocol :
971	
972	1. Request Interception:
973	   - Intercepts WebView requests matching cache patterns
974	   - Handles both HTTP and HTTPS schemes
975	
976	2. Caching Strategy:
977	   - Checks cache before network requests
978	   - Supports conditional requests (ETag, Last-Modified)
979	   - Automatic cache invalidation
980	
981	3. Resource Handling:
982	   - MIME type preservation
983	   - Content validation
984	   - Error handling
985	
986	## Cache Lifecycle
987	
988	The cache implements a sophisticated lifecycle management strategy that balances performance with data freshness:
989	
990	### Content States
991	
992	1. Fresh Content (< 24 hours)
993	   - Content is served directly from cache
994	   - No network requests made
995	   - Fastest possible response time
996	
997	2. Stale Content (24-25 hours)
998	   - Content is served from cache immediately
999	   - Background revalidation is triggered
1000	   - User sees cached content while fresh data is fetched
1001	   - Updates cache if content has changed
1002	
1003	3. Expired Content (> 25 hours)
1004	   - Cache entry is considered invalid
1005	   - Fresh content is fetched from network
1006	   - New cache entry is created
1007	   - User waits for network response
1008	
1009	This stale-while-revalidate pattern provides:
1010	- Optimal user experience with immediate responses
1011	- Efficient network usage
1012	- Up-to-date content without sacrificing performance
1013	- Graceful handling of network issues
1014	
1015	## Best Practices
1016	
1017	1. Cache Pattern Selection:
1018	   - Cache static assets (CSS, JS, images)
1019	   - Avoid caching dynamic content
1020	   - Use specific patterns to prevent over-caching
1021	
1022	2. Development Workflow:
1023	   - Develop with debug builds (`npm run android`, `npm run ios`)
1024	   - Test cache patterns thoroughly in release builds (`npm run android:release`, `npm run ios:release`)
1025	
1026	3. Memory Management:
1027	   - Monitor cache size in low-memory conditions
1028	   - Implement cache cleanup when app goes to background
1029	
1030	### Production vs Development
1031	
1032	Keep one `cachePattern` for both and pick the build with the command:
1033	
1034	```bash
1035	# Development: debug build against the dev server, with HMR
1036	npm run android
1037	npm run ios
1038	
1039	# Production: signed release build
1040	npm run android:release
1041	npm run ios:release
1042	```
1043	
1044	In apps created before Catalyst 1.2.0, run `npm run buildApp:android` and `npm run buildApp:ios`, and add `-- --release` for the release build, for example `npm run buildApp:android -- --release`. Setting `buildType` to `release` still builds a release, with a deprecation warning.
1045

title: Universal App
slug: universal-app
id: universal-app
